n: Elihu begins his second speech, now addressing the wise men listening — perhaps the three friends and any onlookers.
He calls on the wise and knowledgeable to listen carefully.

f.g: Possibly said with a touch of irony toward the friends.

n: Just as the tongue tastes food, the ear tests words to see if they are good. Elihu quotes a saying Job used earlier.
Let’s decide together what is right and figure out what is good.

f.g: Decide for ourselves what is just.

n: Elihu quotes Job: “I am innocent, but God has denied me justice.”

f.w: God hath taken away my judgment

n: Job also said, “Should I lie and admit guilt I don’t have? My wound is incurable, though I have done nothing wrong.”

f.w: Should I lie against my right?
f.g: Should I deny my own innocence?

n: Elihu exaggerates: who is like Job, who gulps down mockery like water?
He claims Job keeps company with evildoers by sharing their views — an unfair overstatement.

f.w: goeth in company with the workers of iniquity

n: Elihu says Job claimed it does no good to please God. Job did say the wicked think this (21:15), but not that he believed it.
Elihu’s main point: it is unthinkable that God would do evil or the Almighty do wrong.

f.w: far be it from God, that he should do wickedness

n: God repays each person according to their deeds and lets them reap what their ways deserve.
Elihu repeats: God will never act wickedly or twist justice.

f.w: neither will the Almighty pervert judgment

n: No one appointed God to rule the earth; he is the original and rightful ruler of everything.

f.g: Set in order, placed in charge of.

n: If God ever decided to take back his spirit and breath…

f.w: if he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath

n: …every living thing would die together and humanity would return to dust. Our very existence depends on God’s goodwill.

f.w: man shall turn again unto dust

n: Elihu turns to Job: if you are wise, listen to this.
Could someone who hates justice govern the universe? Can Job really condemn the One who is perfectly just?
No one dares call even a human king worthless or nobles wicked…

f.w: Is it fit to say to a king

n: …how much less God, who shows no favoritism to princes and doesn’t prefer the rich over the poor, since he made them all.

f.w: accepteth not the persons of princes

n: In an instant the powerful die; whole peoples are shaken at midnight, and the mighty are removed without any human hand.

f.g: Without human agency — by God alone.

n: God’s eyes are on every person’s path, and he sees every step.

f.w: his eyes are upon the ways of man

n: There is no darkness deep enough for evildoers to hide in.
God doesn’t need to schedule a trial with anyone; he already knows everything. (Job had longed for a court date with God.)
He shatters the mighty without lengthy investigation and sets others in their place.
Because he knows their deeds, he overthrows them in the night and they are crushed.
He strikes them down for their wickedness where everyone can see.

f.w: in the open sight of others

n: They turned away from following him and paid no attention to his ways.

f.w: would not consider any of his ways

n: Their oppression made the poor cry out to God, and God heard the cry of the afflicted.

f.w: he heareth the cry of the afflicted

n: If God chooses to stay quiet, who can condemn him? If he hides his face, who can see him? He rules nations and individuals alike.
God acts so that the godless do not rule and trap the people.
Elihu suggests what Job should say to God: “I have endured punishment; I will not offend anymore.”
“Teach me what I can’t see; if I have done wrong, I won’t do it again.” This is a humble prayer, though Elihu assumes Job needs it for sin.

f.w: That which I see not teach thou me

n: Should God reward Job on Job’s terms just because Job rejects God’s way? Job must decide, not Elihu — so let him speak up.
Elihu says sensible people will agree with him.
Elihu concludes that Job has spoken without knowledge or wisdom. God will later make a similar but gentler point (38:2), while still vindicating Job over the friends (42:7).
Elihu wishes Job would be tested to the limit for answering like a wicked man. This is harsh, and the book never shows God endorsing it.
He accuses Job of adding rebellion to sin, clapping his hands in scorn, and piling up words against God.

f.w: he clappeth his hands among us
f.g: Mocks us — a gesture of contempt.
